title: 📘 UNIT 3: SOCIAL, ECONOMIC & POLITICAL DEVELOPMENTS IN ETHIOPIA FROM MID-19th C. TO 1941
3.1 🛤️ LONG-DISTANCE TRADE IN 19th CENTURY ETHIOPIA
notes:
19th-century Ethiopia had extensive long-distance trade that connected peoples and states in the south, north and east.

📌 Trade encouraged interaction among different peoples and political communities while connecting the interior with the Red Sea and Indian Ocean coasts.

🏪 Major market centres included Bonga, Hirmata, Saqa, Asandabo, Basso, Gondar, Adwa, Asmara, Massawa, Soddo, Rogge, Aliyu Amba and Harar.

🛣️ Major routes included:
• Bonga, Hirmata, Saqa, Asandabo, Basso, Gondar and Matamma.
• Gondar, Adwa, Asmara and Massawa.
• Bonga, Hirmata, Soddo, Rogge, Aliyu Amba, Harar and Zeyila or Berbera.

📌 These routes connected the Ethiopian interior with Sudan, the Red Sea and the Somali coast.

title: 3.1.1 💱 MEDIUM OF EXCHANGE & TRADE ITEMS
notes:
💰 Major trade commodities included ivory, civet musk, salt bars known as Amole and slaves.

🧂 Amole consisted of salt bars that were widely used as a medium of exchange.

🪙 Maria Theresa Thaler (MTT) was introduced into the Horn of Africa by Arab traders from Austria at the end of the 18th century and was later used alongside Amole.

📌 Local products from the interior were exchanged in major markets and transported toward coastal trading centres.

title: 3.1.2 👥 PEOPLE INVOLVED IN LONG-DISTANCE TRADE
notes:
Long-distance traders came from different ethnic and religious backgrounds.

👤 Important Muslim merchants included:

• Jabarti, who were northern Muslim merchants.

• Afqala, who were southwestern Muslim Oromo merchants.

• Argoba, who were active in trade between Harar and the northern Somali coast.

🏪 Local peoples also participated actively in trade through individual market centres.

⭐ Importance → Long-distance trade became an important catalyst for interaction and relationships among different peoples and political communities.

title: 3.1.3 ⚒️ COTTAGE INDUSTRY
notes:
Cottage industry refers to traditional small-scale production and handicraft activities carried out by local artisans.

📜 Cottage industries and handicraft technologies had existed in Ethiopia since ancient times.

🏠 Major cottage industries included:
• Metalworking.
• Pottery.
• Tannery.
• Carpentry.
• Masonry.
• Weaving.
• Jewellery making.
• Basket making.

⚠️ Social problem → Artisans were often disdained and marginalized.

📌 Result → The production of agricultural tools and household goods remained relatively limited in development and sophistication.

title: 3.1.4 🔨 BLACKSMITHING & ITS IMPORTANCE
notes:
Blacksmiths produced goods that were important for agriculture, household activities, the economy and military affairs.

🌾 Agricultural tools included ploughshares, pick-axe parts, sickles and other implements.

🏠 Household products included knives, razors, pans, nails, hatchets, saws, files, chains and rings.

⚔️ Military products included spearheads, daggers, swords, bullets and rifle spare parts.

🐎 Other products included tent-pegs, hammers, pincers, drills, fire steels, horse and mule bits and stirrups.

⭐ Importance → Blacksmithing supported agriculture, household life, trade, military activities and the wider Ethiopian economy.

title: 3.2 👑 MAKING OF THE MODERN ETHIOPIAN STATE (1855–1913)
notes:
The making of the modern Ethiopian state involved three major processes:

🏛️ Unification involved bringing northern and north-central regions under stronger central authority.

🗺️ Territorial expansion extended imperial authority into southern and southwestern regions.

⚙️ Modernization introduced administrative, military, technological and socio-economic reforms.

👑 Major rulers included Tewodros II, Yohannes IV and Menilek II.

📌 Modern state formation developed through centralization, unification, territorial expansion and modernization.

title: 3.2.1 👑 TEWODROS II: UNIFICATION & CENTRALIZATION
notes:
👤 Kassa Hailu was the ruler of Quara before becoming Emperor Tewodros II in 1855.

⚔️ Before his coronation, Kassa defeated several major regional rulers:
• Dejjazmach Goshu Zewde at Gur Amba in 1852.
• Birru Aligaz and other Dejjazmachs at Gorgora Bichegn in 1853.
• Ras Ali of Yejju at Ayshal on 29 June 1853.
• Dejjazmach Wube of Semen and Tigray at Deresge on 8 February 1855.

⭐ Battle of Ayshal symbolized the end of the Zemene Mesafint.

📅 On 9 February 1855, Kassa Hailu was crowned Emperor Tewodros II.

🎯 His main vision was to create a territorially united, militarily strong and self-dependent Ethiopia.

title: 3.2.2 ⚔️ TEWODROS II'S CAMPAIGNS
notes:
🇪🇹 Wallo Campaign → The campaign began in March 1855, and Tewodros captured Maqdala on 12 September 1855.

🇪🇹 Shewa Campaign → The campaign lasted about five months, and Shewan forces were defeated at Bereket in November 1855.

📌 After the Shewa campaign, rebellions continued in areas such as Gojjam and Semen.

⚠️ Significance → The end of the Shewan campaign marked the peak of Tewodros's power and was followed by the gradual decline of his reign.

title: 3.2.3 ⚙️ TEWODROS II'S REFORMS & MODERNIZATION
notes:
⚔️ Military reforms included introducing military ranks such as Yasr Aleqa, Yamsa Aleqa and Yeshi Aleqa.

🎖️ Tewodros also attempted to replace regional armies with a salaried national army.

🏭 Arms production → He established an arms workshop at Gafat near Debre Tabor with assistance from European missionaries and artisans.

💣 Gafat produced about 35 cannons, including the famous mortar known as Sebastopol.

⛪ Church and land reform → Tewodros confiscated some church land in order to distribute land to landless people. He also reduced the number of priests and deacons in each church to five.

🎯 Overall goal → His reforms aimed to strengthen central government, modernize the army and increase national self-reliance.

title: 3.2.4 ⚠️ CHALLENGES TO TEWODROS II
notes:
🏛️ Internal opposition → Regional rulers resisted centralization because they wanted to preserve their local power.

⛪ Clergy also opposed Tewodros because of his interference in church affairs.

🌍 External problem → Britain did not provide the assistance Tewodros expected for modernization.

🇬🇧 Conflict with Britain → After failing to receive satisfactory responses to his requests, Tewodros detained Europeans.

⚔️ British Expedition → Britain sent a large military expedition after negotiations failed.

📅 30 April 1868 → British forces stormed Maqdala.

📅 13 April 1868 → Tewodros committed suicide at Maqdala.

📌 Result → His reign ended and his major centralization and modernization projects were interrupted.

title: 3.2.5 👑 YOHANNES IV: DECENTRALIZED RULE
notes:
👤 Kassa Mircha became Emperor Yohannes IV from 1872 to 1889 after defeating Tekle-Giorgis II at Assem in 1871.

🏛️ Administrative approach → Yohannes introduced a relatively decentralized system and allowed regional rulers considerable autonomy.

📜 Liche Agreement of 1878 → Yohannes recognized Menilek as Nigus, or King, of Shewa.

📜 In 1881 → Ras Adal Tesema of Gojjam was designated Nigus Tekle-Haymanot of Gojjam and Kafa.

🤝 Yohannes achieved unity among many predominantly Christian provinces, including Wag and Lasta, Simen, Begemdir, Amhara Saynt, Gojjam, Wallo, Shewa and Mereb Milash.

📌 Main difference → Tewodros emphasized strong centralization, while Yohannes allowed greater regional autonomy while maintaining imperial authority.

title: 3.2.6 ⛪ COUNCIL OF BORU MEDA: 1878
notes:
📍 Boru Meda was the site of an important religious council during the reign of Yohannes IV.

🎯 Purpose → The council addressed religious controversy within the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahdo Church.

📜 Decision → Tewahdo was declared the only doctrine of the Ethiopian Orthodox Church.

⚠️ Effect on Muslims → Some Ethiopian Muslims, particularly in Wallo, were forced to convert to Orthodox Christianity.

➡️ Responses → Some converted superficially, while others migrated to areas such as Arsi, Gurage, Jimma and Sudan.

📌 Important figures → Mohammed Ali became Ras Mikael, while Amede Liban became Dejjach Hayle-Mariam after conversion.

title: 3.2.7 🗺️ MENILEK II: TERRITORIAL EXPANSION
notes:
👑 Menilek II continued the formation of the modern Ethiopian state through territorial expansion and modernization.

📅 His expansion can be divided into three phases:
1️⃣ 1865–1889 → Menilek ruled as King of Shewa.
2️⃣ 1889–1896 → From his coronation as Emperor until the Battle of Adwa.
3️⃣ 1896–1900 → The period following the victory at Adwa.

📌 Expansion → Some territories submitted peacefully, while others were incorporated through military conquest.

👤 Ras Gobana Dache played a major role in the incorporation of many territories during Menilek's expansion.

title: 3.2.8 🌍 FIRST PHASE OF MENILEK'S EXPANSION
notes:
📅 1865–1889 → During this period Menilek ruled as King of Shewa.

🌍 Areas incorporated included Tulama, eastern Macha Oromo territories, northern Gurage and other surrounding areas.

🤝 Peaceful submission → Kistane or Soddo Gurage submitted without resistance.

⚔️ Resistance → Western Gurage under Hassan Enjamo of Qabena resisted until Ras Gobana defeated them in 1888.

📌 Major figures → Menilek II and Ras Gobana Dache played leading roles in this phase.

title: 3.2.9 ⚔️ WESTERN & SOUTHWESTERN EXPANSION
notes:
🌍 Expansion south of the Abay River included Horro Guduru, Leqa-Naqamte, Leqa-Qellem and Jimma.

⚔️ Battle of Embabo → Ras Adal or Tekle-Haymanot was defeated by Menilek's commander Ras Gobana.

🤝 After Embabo → Leqa-Naqamte, Leqa-Qellem and Jimma Abba Jifar submitted peacefully and were promised recognition while maintaining a degree of autonomy.

⚔️ Arsi Oromo → They resisted strongly, and Menilek conducted six campaigns between 1882 and 1886.

📅 Battle of Azule → On 6 September 1886, Arsi resistance was suppressed by Ras Darge Sahla Sellasie.

⚔️ Hararghe → Harari and Oromo forces resisted imperial expansion.

📅 Battle of Chalanqo → On 6 January 1887, the resistance was defeated.

👤 Dejjach Mekonnen Welde-Mikael was appointed governor of Hararghe.

title: 3.2.10 🌾 GREAT FAMINE & FURTHER EXPANSION
notes:
📅 Kefu Qan, or the Great Famine, occurred from 1888 to 1892.

🦠 Immediate cause → A rinderpest epidemic associated with infected cattle imported through Massawa.

🐄 Effect → The epidemic devastated the country and greatly reduced cattle populations.

📌 Political consequence → The crisis partly encouraged and gave momentum to Menilek's territorial expansion in southern Ethiopia.

📅 Between 1889 and 1894 → Dawuro, Konta, Kambata, Bale, Sidama, Gamo Gofa and Wolaita were incorporated.

⚔️ Wolaita → Strong resistance was suppressed in 1894, and Kawo Tona, the last king of Wolaita, was arrested.

➡️ Later incorporated → Gedeo, Borana and Konso were also brought under Menilek's authority.

title: 3.2.11 🗺️ FINAL TERRITORIAL EXPANSION & BOUNDARIES
notes:
📅 1897 → Kafa was incorporated after Tato Gaki Sherocho was defeated by Menilek's army led by Ras Wolde Giorgis.

🌍 Menilek also extended authority over Benishangul and Gambella.

📜 Boundary agreements → Ethiopia concluded agreements with surrounding colonial powers between 1897 and 1908.

🗺️ Major agreements included:
• French Somaliland or Djibouti → 20 March 1897.
• British Somaliland → May 1897.
• Italian Eritrea → 10 July 1900.
• Anglo-Egyptian Sudan → 15 May 1902.
• British East Africa or Kenya → 1907.
• Italian Somaliland → 1908.

⭐ Significance → These agreements gave Ethiopia approximately its present territorial shape, although many boundaries were mapped rather than fully demarcated on the ground.

title: 3.2.12 🏙️ MENILEK II'S MODERNIZATION
notes:
🏦 Bank of Abyssinia → Established in 1905 and became the first modern bank.

🏫 Menilek II School → Established in 1908 and became the first modern school.

📮 Postal system → Ethiopia introduced its first modern postal service.

🚂 Railway → An agreement with the French was initiated in 1894 for the Addis Ababa–Djibouti railway project.

💡 Modern technology → Electricity, telephone, telegraph, motor cars and modern plumbing were introduced.

🪙 Currency → Menilek began minting coins to replace the Maria Theresa Thaler.

⭐ Overall → Menilek combined territorial expansion with technological, economic and administrative modernization.

title: 3.3 ⚔️ EXTERNAL AGGRESSIONS & UNITY OF ETHIOPIAN PEOPLE (1871–1896)
notes:
During the second half of the 19th century, Ethiopian independence faced several major external threats.

🇬🇧 Britain → Sent a military expedition against Tewodros II.

🇪🇬 Egypt → Attempted to expand into Ethiopia and control the Nile basin.

🇸🇩 Mahdists → Fought Ethiopia along the Sudanese frontier.

🇮🇹 Italy → Attempted to establish colonial control over northern Ethiopia.

⭐ Ethiopian response → Military resistance and national mobilization helped defend territorial integrity and sovereignty.

title: 3.3.1 🇬🇧 BRITISH NAPIER EXPEDITION: 1867–1868
notes:
📌 Background → Tewodros II wanted British military and technical assistance against Egypt and for modernization.

📜 1862 → Tewodros sent a letter to Queen Victoria requesting assistance.

❌ Problem → His request received no satisfactory response.

👤 Consul Cameron → Tewodros blamed him for the failure to receive a response and suspected a foreign conspiracy.

🇬🇧 Britain → Decided to send a military expedition to free Europeans detained by Tewodros.

👤 Commander → Sir Robert Napier.

⚔️ Battle of Aroge → On 10 April 1868, Ethiopian forces were defeated.

📅 11 April 1868 → Tewodros released the European captives.

📅 13 April 1868 → Tewodros committed suicide at Maqdala.

🔥 Afterward → Maqdala was burned and treasures were looted.

📌 Britain did not remain in Ethiopia and withdrew after accomplishing its main objective.

title: 3.3.2 🇪🇬 EGYPTIAN AGGRESSION
notes:
🎯 Egyptian ambition → Egypt wanted to control Northeast Africa and the source of the Nile.

📅 1875 → Khedive Ismail Pasha launched an invasion of Ethiopia through three directions.

1️⃣ Zeila Front → Mohammed Rauf Pasha led the Egyptian forces, which occupied the Harar Emirate from 1875 to 1885.

2️⃣ Tajura Front → Werner Munzinger led the forces, but they were annihilated by the Afar.

3️⃣ Massawa Front → Colonel Arendrup and Arakel Bey led about 2,000 troops.

🇪🇹 Ethiopian response → Emperor Yohannes IV and Ras Alula mobilized about 20,000 troops.

🏆 Battle of Gundat → On 16 November 1875, Egypt suffered a severe defeat.

🏆 Battle of Gura → From 7 to 9 March 1876, Egyptian forces were defeated again.

📌 Result → Egyptian attempts to conquer Ethiopia failed.

title: 3.3.3 🛡️ HEWETT TREATY & MAHDIST CONFLICT
notes:
🇸🇩 Mahdist movement → The Sudanese struggle against Egyptian rule forced Egyptian troops into the Kassala area.

📜 Hewett Treaty → In 1884, Britain brokered an agreement between Ethiopia and Egypt.

🤝 Ethiopian agreement → Ethiopia agreed to help evacuate Egyptian soldiers surrounded by Mahdists in eastern Sudan.

🎁 In return → Ethiopia received, among other benefits, use or access to Massawa.

⚠️ Consequence → Ethiopian involvement angered the Mahdists and contributed to armed conflict between Ethiopia and the Mahdists.

⚔️ Kufit → In September 1885, Ethiopian forces won.

⚔️ Sar Wuha → In 1888, Mahdist forces defeated the troops of Nigus Tekle-Haymanot in Dembia.

⚠️ Yohannes faced a triangular tension involving Italians in the north, Mahdists in the west and northwest, and internal challenges from Menilek and Tekle-Haymanot.

title: 3.3.4 🛡️ DEATH OF YOHANNES IV
notes:
📅 9 March 1889 → Emperor Yohannes IV marched to Metemma against the Mahdists.

⚔️ Battle of Metemma → Yohannes was killed while fighting the Mahdists.

📌 Significance → Ethiopia lost a major ruler while facing external threats and internal political tensions.

⭐ Lesson → Foreign aggression and internal divisions created serious challenges to national unity and Ethiopian sovereignty.

title: 3.3.5 🇮🇹 ITALIAN ENCROACHMENT
notes:
🇮🇹 Italy became the most dangerous foreign power challenging Ethiopia during the late 19th century.

📅 1869 → The opening of the Suez Canal increased the strategic and commercial importance of the Red Sea.

⚓ Assab → The Italian Rubatino shipping company acquired the port from local chiefs in 1869, and it was transferred to the Italian government in 1882.

⚓ Massawa → Britain secretly transferred Massawa from Egypt to Italy in 1885.

🗺️ Italian aim → Italy sought to expand from its coastal bases into northern Ethiopia and Mereb Milash.

🏆 Battle of Dogali → In 1887, Ethiopian forces led by Ras Alula decisively defeated the Italians.

title: 3.3.6 📜 TREATY OF WUCHALE: 1889
notes:
📅 2 May 1889 → The Treaty of Wuchale was signed between Menilek II and Italian representative Count Pietro Antonelli.

🎯 Purpose → The treaty was intended to promote friendship and trade between Ethiopia and Italy.

⚠️ Main problem → Differences existed between the Amharic and Italian versions of the treaty.

📜 Article XVII → The Amharic version stated that Ethiopia could use Italy's good offices when dealing with foreign powers, while the Italian version made this an obligation.

🇮🇹 Italian interpretation → Italy used the Italian version to claim that Ethiopia had accepted Italian protection.

❌ Menilek → He rejected the Italian interpretation and unilaterally abrogated the treaty in 1893.

📌 Result → The dispute contributed directly to the First Italo-Ethiopian War.

title: 3.3.7 🏆 BATTLE OF ADWA: 1 MARCH 1896
notes:
🔥 Cause → Italy attempted to expand colonial control over Ethiopia, while the dispute over the Treaty of Wuchale increased tensions.

📢 Menilek's mobilization → He called on Ethiopians to defend their country and religion.

👥 About 100,000 Ethiopian troops gathered from different parts of the country.

🤝 Participation → People mobilized across regional, ethnic and gender differences.

⚔️ Major Ethiopian leaders included Menilek II, Empress Taytu, Ras Mikael, Ras Makonnen, Ras Alula, Ras Mangasha and Nigus Tekle-Haymanot.

🏆 Preliminary victories → Ethiopian forces achieved victories at Amba-Alage and Mekelle.

📅 1 March 1896 → The decisive Battle of Adwa was fought.

🇪🇹 Result → Ethiopia achieved a historic victory over Italy.

⚔️ Casualties → About 8,000 Italian soldiers were killed, 1,500 were wounded and 3,000 were captured. Ethiopian losses were approximately 4,000 to 6,000.

title: 3.3.8 🌍 SIGNIFICANCE OF ADWA
notes:
🇪🇹 Ethiopian independence → Italy recognized Ethiopia as an independent and sovereign state.

📜 Treaty of Addis Ababa → Signed on 26 October 1896, it ended the war.

🌍 International recognition → France, Britain, Russia, the United States, Germany, Belgium and Turkey recognized Ethiopia and established diplomatic missions in Addis Ababa.

🤝 National unity → Cooperation among Ethiopia's peoples contributed to national integration.

✊ African significance → Adwa became a powerful symbol of African resistance, independence and anti-colonial struggle.

⭐ Global meaning → The victory became one of the most important victories achieved by an African army against a major European colonial power.

title: 3.4 👑 POWER STRUGGLE AMONG RULING ELITES (1906–1935)
notes:
📅 1906 → A major turning point in Ethiopia's post-Adwa political history.

👑 Menilek II → Suffered his first stroke.

⚰️ Ras Mekonnen → Died in the same year and had been expected by many to succeed Menilek.

⚠️ Result → Succession and power struggles intensified.

🌍 Tripartite Treaty of 1906 → Britain, France and Italy reached an agreement based on their interests in Ethiopia and surrounding regions.

🎯 Main interests included:
• Britain → Nile basin.
• France → Railway zone.
• Italy → Hinterlands of Eritrea and Italian Somaliland.

title: 3.4.1 🏛️ MENILEK II'S SUCCESSION MEASURES
notes:
🏛️ 1907 → Menilek established Ethiopia's first cabinet, or Ministers' Council.

🎯 Purpose → The cabinet was partly intended to address the succession problem and possible power vacuum.

👑 1909 → Menilek named his grandson Lij Iyasu as successor and regent.

👸 Empress Taytu → Her political influence increased after Menilek became seriously ill.

⚠️ Opposition → Shewan nobles opposed her growing influence and forced her to withdraw from politics in 1910.

title: 3.4.2 👑 LIJ IYASU: 1911–1916
notes:
📅 1911–1916 → Lij Iyasu exercised de facto political power.

⚙️ Policies and reforms included:
• Continuing Menilek's modernization program.
• Establishing Addis Ababa's first police force.
• Attempting to reform property ownership.
• Attempting taxation reforms.
• Removing the traditional Quragna system.
• Banning the Lebashay institution.

📌 Iyasu introduced bold and progressive policies, but these policies created opposition among internal and external forces.

📅 27 September 1916 → Lij Iyasu was deposed.

👸 Zewditu → Menilek's daughter became Empress.

👤 Ras Teferi Mekonnen → He was promoted to Ras and named successor to the throne.

title: 3.4.3 ⚔️ BATTLE OF SAGALE: 1916
notes:
👤 After Iyasu's deposition → His father, Nigus Mikael, attempted to reverse the palace coup.

⚔️ Battle of Sagale → Fought on 27 October 1916.

🇪🇹 Nigus Mikael's forces → They were defeated by the Shewan army led by Ras Teferi.

📌 Significance → The battle confirmed the political settlement created after Iyasu's deposition.

⭐ Result → Zewditu remained Empress, while Ras Teferi became the powerful heir and regent.

title: 3.4.4 ⚖️ DIARCHY: 1916–1930
notes:
Diarchy was a system of dual governance in which Empress Zewditu and Ras Teferi Mekonnen shared political authority.

👸 Conservative camp → Supporters of Empress Zewditu and traditional political interests.

👤 Leader → Fitawrari Habte Giyorgis Dinagde.

👤 Progressive camp → Supporters of Ras Teferi and modernization.

⚔️ Main feature → Continuous political struggle occurred between conservative and progressive forces.

📈 Teferi's power gradually increased.

📅 1918 → Most ministers were expelled except Habte Giyorgis, strengthening Teferi's position.

📅 December 1926 → Habte Giyorgis died, weakening the conservative camp.

⚔️ Challenges → Dejjach Balcha Safo and Ras Gugsa Wale openly challenged Teferi.

📅 1928 → Balcha Safo was removed from his governorship.

🏆 Battle of Anchim in 1930 → Ras Gugsa Wale was defeated.

📌 End → Teferi gained effective control of the state.

title: 3.4.5 👑 HAILE SELASSIE I & THE 1931 CONSTITUTION
notes:
📅 1928 → Ras Teferi was crowned Nigus.

📅 1930 → He became Emperor Haile Selassie I.

🎯 Main objective → Consolidate centralized and autocratic imperial power.

📜 1931 Constitution → Ethiopia's first written constitution.

🏛️ Powers of the Emperor included:
• Appointing and dismissing officials.
• Administering justice.
• Declaring and ending wars.
• Granting lands and honours.

📌 Political effect → The constitution strengthened imperial authority and provided a legal basis for the emerging absolutist system.

title: 3.4.6 🏛️ CENTRALIZATION & MILITARY REFORMS UNDER HAILE SELASSIE
notes:
🏛️ Provincial autonomy → Hereditary aristocrats lost much of their political influence.

📌 Exception → Tigray retained rule by descendants of local hereditary chiefs.

➡️ Other provinces → They were increasingly governed by officials directly appointed by the Emperor.

⚔️ Imperial Bodyguard → Belgian officers began training the Imperial Bodyguard in 1930.

🎖️ Holeta Military Training → The first officer training school was established in 1934 by a Swedish military mission.

📌 Importance → These reforms strengthened the national army and imperial central authority.

⚠️ Italian invasion → The invasion interrupted the first officer training program, and many cadets later became committed patriots.

title: 3.5 🇮🇹 FASCIST ITALIAN AGGRESSION & PATRIOTIC RESISTANCE
notes:
🇮🇹 Italy → Italy did not abandon its ambition to colonize Ethiopia after its defeat at Adwa.

👤 Benito Mussolini → The Fascist leader came to power in Italy in 1922.

🎯 Mussolini's goal → He wanted to restore the glory and power associated with ancient Rome and expand Italian influence in Africa.

📌 Ethiopia → Became the target of a major Italian military campaign.

⚔️ Immediate pretext → The Walwal clash of 5 December 1934 between Ethiopian and Italian forces in the Ogaden occurred over an ill-defined border.

title: 3.5.1 ⚔️ SECOND ITALO-ETHIOPIAN WAR: 1935–1936
notes:
📅 3 October 1935 → Italian forces crossed the Mereb or Marab River and invaded Ethiopia.

🇮🇹 Northern Front → Initially commanded by Emilio de Bono and later by Pietro Badoglio.

🇮🇹 Southern Front → Commanded by Marshal Rodolfo Graziani.

💣 Italian advantages included:
• Modern weapons.
• Large military forces.
• Air superiority.
• Poison gas and chemical weapons.
• Better preparation and supplies.

🇪🇹 Ethiopian response → The Emperor's mobilization order produced a large national response.

⚠️ Delay in Ethiopian counter-offensive → Ethiopia partly hoped that the League of Nations and international community would provide justice, while Italian forces were allowed to move deeper into the country.

title: 3.5.2 🛡️ NORTHERN FRONT
notes:
👤 Overall Ethiopian commander → Ras Kassa Hailu.

👥 Major commanders included:
• Ras Mulugeta Yeggezu, who was Minister of War.
• Ras Seyoum Mengesha, who ruled Tigray.
• Ras Emeru Haile-Selassie, who governed Gojjam.

⚔️ Major battles included Tembien, Amba Aradom, Shire and Maychew.

🏆 Shire → Ethiopian forces achieved a limited victory.

❌ Tembien and Amba Aradom → Italian forces achieved victories.

⚰️ Ras Mulugeta Yeggezu → He was killed during the fighting.

📅 31 March 1936 → Battle of Maychew. Emperor Haile Selassie led the remaining troops and Imperial Bodyguard.

❌ Result → Italy won because of strong fortifications and overwhelming air superiority.

title: 3.5.3 🌍 SOUTHERN FRONT & FALL OF ADDIS ABABA
notes:
🇪🇹 Southern Ethiopian commanders included Ras Desta Damtew, Dejjach Nesibu Zeamanuel, Dejazmach Balcha Safo and Dejjach or Ras-bitwadad Mekonnen Endalkachew.

📍 Main areas → Ogaden, Sidamo and Bale.

❌ Result → Ethiopian forces could not stop Graziani's advance.

📅 2 May 1936 → Emperor Haile Selassie and his royal family left Addis Ababa for Europe through Djibouti.

📅 5 May 1936 → Addis Ababa was occupied by Italian forces under Marshal Badoglio.

🏙️ Harar → Captured shortly after Addis Ababa.

📌 Italy → Achieved military occupation of most of Ethiopia.

title: 3.5.4 💣 WHY ITALY DEFEATED ETHIOPIA IN 1936
notes:
🇮🇹 Italian advantages included:
• Superior weapons.
• Large and well-prepared forces.
• Air superiority.
• Use of internationally banned mustard or poison gas.
• Better logistical organization.

🇪🇹 Ethiopian difficulties included:
• Poor roads.
• Limited radio communication.
• Lack of accurate maps.
• Logistical problems.
• A military system transitioning from feudal organization to modern warfare.
• Traditional military courage that was not matched by modern military technology and skills.

📌 Key comparison → At Adwa in 1896, Ethiopia achieved decisive military success, while in 1936 Italy possessed overwhelming technological, logistical and air superiority.

title: 3.5.5 🇮🇹 ITALIAN EAST AFRICA (AOI)
notes:
📅 1936 → Italian-occupied Ethiopia was combined with Eritrea and Somalia.

📛 New colonial territory → Italian East Africa, also called Africa Orientale Italiana or AOI.

🗺️ Six major divisions included:
1️⃣ Eritrea, including Tigray, with Asmara as capital.
2️⃣ Amhara, including Begemdir, Gojjam, Wallo and northern Shewa, with Gondar as capital.
3️⃣ Addis Ababa, which was later renamed Shewa.
4️⃣ Oromo and Sidama, with Jimma as capital.
5️⃣ Harar.
6️⃣ Somalia, including Ogaden, with Mogadishu as capital.

👤 Viceroys → Badoglio served first, followed by Graziani, and later Amadeo Umberto d'Aosta ruled until Italy's surrender in 1941.

title: 3.5.6 🛡️ ETHIOPIAN PATRIOTS: ARBEGNOCH
notes:
🇪🇹 Patriots, or Arbegnoch, were Ethiopian resistance fighters who fought against Italian occupation.

📌 Resistance → The resistance began almost immediately after the Italian occupation.

👥 Character → It spread across many regions and involved people from different ethnic communities.

🎯 Goal → Patriots fought to resist Italian colonial rule and restore Ethiopian independence.

🤝 National resistance → Despite Italian attempts to divide the Patriots, resistance involved people from many parts of Ethiopia.

⭐ Significance → The patriotic resistance preserved the spirit of Ethiopian independence throughout the occupation and contributed to the restoration of Ethiopian sovereignty in 1941.

title: 🏆 UNIT 3: MUST REMEMBER
notes:
🛤️ LONG-DISTANCE TRADE

Major routes included Bonga, Hirmata, Saqa, Asandabo, Basso, Gondar and Matamma; Gondar, Adwa, Asmara and Massawa; and Bonga, Hirmata, Soddo, Rogge, Aliyu Amba, Harar and Zeyila or Berbera.

Major traders included Jabarti, Afqala and Argoba.

Major commodities included ivory, civet musk, Amole and slaves.

Mediums of exchange included Amole and the Maria Theresa Thaler.

⚒️ COTTAGE INDUSTRY

Major activities included metalworking, pottery, tannery, carpentry, masonry, weaving, jewellery making and basket making.

Blacksmiths produced agricultural tools, household goods, weapons and military equipment.

👑 MODERN ETHIOPIAN STATE

Tewodros II focused on centralization, a national army and modernization, including the Gafat arms workshop and the production of Sebastopol.

Yohannes IV followed a more decentralized system, supported religious unification through the Council of Boru Meda and resisted Egypt, the Mahdists and Italy.

Menilek II expanded Ethiopian territory and introduced important technological, economic and administrative reforms.

⚔️ KEY BATTLES

Ayshal, 1853 → Helped end the Zemene Mesafint.

Aroge, 1868 → British forces defeated Tewodros's army.

Gundat, 1875 → Ethiopia defeated Egypt.

Gura, 1876 → Ethiopia defeated Egypt again.

Kufit, 1885 → Ethiopia defeated the Mahdists.

Dogali, 1887 → Ras Alula defeated Italian forces.

Metemma, 1889 → Yohannes IV was killed fighting the Mahdists.

Adwa, 1 March 1896 → Ethiopia decisively defeated Italy.

Anchim, 1930 → Ras Gugsa Wale was defeated.

Maychew, 31 March 1936 → Italy defeated Ethiopian forces.

📜 KEY TREATIES & AGREEMENTS

Liche Agreement, 1878 → Yohannes recognized Menilek as Nigus of Shewa.

Hewett Treaty, 1884 → Ethiopia agreed to help evacuate Egyptian troops, which contributed to conflict with the Mahdists.

Wuchale Treaty, 1889 → The Article XVII dispute contributed to war with Italy.

Addis Ababa Treaty, 26 October 1896 → Italy recognized Ethiopian independence.

⚖️ POWER STRUGGLE

1906 → Menilek suffered a stroke and Ras Mekonnen died, creating a succession crisis.

1907 → Menilek established the first cabinet.

1909 → Lij Iyasu was named successor.

1916 → Iyasu was deposed, Zewditu became Empress and Ras Teferi became heir and regent.

1916–1930 → Diarchy between Zewditu and Ras Teferi.

1928 → Ras Teferi was crowned Nigus.

1930 → Ras Teferi became Emperor Haile Selassie I.

1931 → Ethiopia adopted its first written constitution.

🇮🇹 ITALIAN AGGRESSION

5 December 1934 → Walwal clash.

3 October 1935 → Italy invaded Ethiopia.

31 March 1936 → Battle of Maychew.

2 May 1936 → Haile Selassie left Ethiopia.

5 May 1936 → Addis Ababa was occupied.

1936 → Italian East Africa was created.

1941 → Italian rule ended and Ethiopian sovereignty was restored.
